results.title: Seoul district prepares to bring pet funerals directly to residents' doors
results.content: Courier scooters in Seoul deliver everything from midnight kimchi stew to designer handbags in under an hour, and soon grieving pet owners in the city's east will be able to summon a hearse just as easily. Starting in December, Seongdong District, located just east of downtown Seoul, will roll out a municipal mobile pet funeral service, dispatching specialized vans to residents' homes to collect deceased pets, hold a memorial ceremony and perform odorless, smoke-free cremations before returning the ashes in an urn. The initiative, finalized through a partnership signed earlier this month between the district office and local pet funeral operator Petmoon, tackles a thorny urban dilemma in Korea’s densely packed capital. results.title: Herbalife Korea builds next chapter on 30 years of trust
results.content: Herbalife Korea’s next phase of growth will depend on lasting customer relationships rather than individual transactions, Herbalife Korea General Manager Sean Chung said, as the company marks its 30th anniversary in Korea by overhauling distributor compensation and introducing AI tools. The company’s history has been about helping Koreans build healthy nutrition habits, he said, arguing that sustainable growth comes from maintaining trust beyond a single sale. Since entering Korea in 1996, Herbalife has expanded from weight management products into everyday nutrition, protein, sports nutrition and beauty-related wellness as consumer priorities have evolved. Its first decade centered on its flagship Formula 1 shake brand, balancing nutrient intake and healthy eating habits in a market dominated by physical stores and face-to-face sales. results.title: Mountain festival brings foreign tourists to Seoul's peaks
results.content: In a sprawling metropolis better known globally for neon-lit shopping districts, K-pop studios and royal palaces, some of Seoul’s hottest tourist attractions this fall required sturdy boots and a willingness to work up a sweat. More than 13,000 hikers passed through Seoul’s mountain tourism centers during the three weeks of 2026 Seoul Hiking Week, which wrapped up Sunday, underscoring how Korea’s capital is successfully turning its rugged granite peaks into an urban playground. According to the Seoul Tourism Organization, which hosted the third edition of the autumn festival starting on Oct. 26, roughly 4,800 of the visitors to its three Seoul Hiking Tourism Centers were foreign nationals — a 48 percent jump from the same period in 2025. results.title: More Chinese than Korean members: Why K-pop is becoming more multicultural
results.content: Six. That is the number of Chinese members in A2O Soul, the new group recently launched by producer Lee Soo-man's A2O Entertainment as he returns to Korea's K-pop market after a three-year hiatus. The multinational group consists of 15 members, with Chinese nationals accounting for 40 percent, the largest share of any nationality. Korean nationals, including those with dual citizenship, make up five members, or 33.3 percent. It is the first time a K-pop group debuting in Korea has more Chinese members than Korean ones. Multinational groups are nothing new in K-pop. However, among groups debuting in Korea, rather than overseas-localized acts, Korean members have traditionally made up the largest nationality group. results.title: Why are young Koreans falling for Japanese animated series 'Chiikawa?'
results.content: "I'm worried everything will sell out. They'll keep restocking, right?" A long line of customers stretched outside the Chiikawa Shop on the third floor of I'Park Mall in Yongsan District, Seoul, Nov. 5. A quick count put the number of people waiting at well over 50. They had come to buy merchandise featuring characters from the Japanese animated series "Chiikawa." One shopper, surnamed Kim, 27, emerged carrying a large bag filled with stuffed toys, figurines and key rings. "I came to love the animation because I find hope in the way Chiikawa overcomes life's hardships and grows along the way," Kim said with a laugh. "I kept adding things to my basket and ended up spending 460,000 won ($315)."
